keep: Map the deaths house by house. Data collected with your own shoes beats a beautiful theory.
lede: The science that tracks every epidemic — including the most recent pandemic — effectively begins with him.
copy: A self-made physician and pioneering anesthesiologist who gave Queen Victoria chloroform in childbirth, Snow rejected the reigning theory that cholera spread through foul air, or “miasma”.

During a savage 1854 outbreak in London's Soho he did something radical: he gathered data. He mapped the deaths house by house and found them clustered around a single public water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the parish authorities to remove the pump handle — years before the germ that causes cholera was even seen.

Snow died at forty-five, his water theory still disputed. But his method — reasoning from carefully collected population data to the cause of disease — founded modern epidemiology and has since saved more lives than almost any battlefield victory.

bio.why: Turns the 1854 Broad Street outbreak into a gripping detective story, following Snow and the local curate Henry Whitehead as they crack the case. It doubles as a meditation on cities, data and disease.

contested: The story everyone tells (Snow removed the handle and stopped the outbreak) is not what the evidence shows. Whitehead's own data had fatal attacks falling from 142 on 1 September to 14 by 8 September, the day the handle came off: the outbreak was already collapsing. Snow himself never claimed the removal ended it. Whitehead's argument was subtler and better — that removal probably prevented a second outbreak, since the index case's father fell ill that same day.
